questions.question: Explain how to read a world climate map and how to describe the distribution of a climate region.
questions.expected_answer: Read the key first, because colours differ between atlases. Locate the equator, the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn at about 23.5 degrees and the polar circles at about 66.5 degrees. Identify continents and oceans and the side of each continent, since east and west coasts at the same latitude differ because of currents and winds. To describe distribution, give latitudes, continents and countries, the side of the continent, and links with physical features, with two or three examples, for example: the Mediterranean climate lies at about 30 to 45 degrees on western sides of continents, around the Mediterranean, California, central Chile, the south-western Cape and south-western Australia. Remember maps simplify gradual change, and vegetation maps match climate maps closely.

questions.question: Describe the global sequence of climate belts from the equator to the poles, with examples.
questions.expected_answer: Tropical rainforest within about 10 degrees of the equator: Amazon, Congo Basin, Indonesia; monsoon in South and South-East Asia and West Africa. Tropical savanna at about 5 to 20 degrees: much of Africa south of the Sahara, Brazilian highlands, northern Australia, India. Hot desert and semi-desert at about 15 to 35 degrees: Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Kalahari, Namib, Australian, Atacama, with the Sahel and Karoo around them. At about 30 to 45 degrees, Mediterranean on western sides and humid subtropical on eastern sides, such as KwaZulu-Natal and south-eastern China. At about 40 to 60 degrees, temperate oceanic on western sides, such as north-western Europe, and continental interiors with taiga in North America and Eurasia. Beyond about 60 degrees, tundra around the Arctic, and ice caps on Greenland and Antarctica. High mountain climates cut across: Andes, Rockies, Himalayas, Ethiopian and Lesotho highlands.

questions.question: Describe the climate regions of South Africa and explain the east-to-west rainfall pattern.
questions.expected_answer: West coast: desert, the Namib extending into the Richtersveld and Namaqualand, caused by the cold Benguela Current and South Atlantic high pressure. Interior west: semi-desert Karoo and Kalahari. East and north: summer-rainfall grassland on the highveld and savanna in Limpopo and Mpumalanga. East coast: humid subtropical KwaZulu-Natal and northern Eastern Cape with the warm Agulhas Current. South-west: Mediterranean winter rainfall around Cape Town. Southern coast: rain in all seasons. Drakensberg and Lesotho: high mountain with winter snow. Rainfall decreases from over 1 000 mm in the east and on the escarpment to under 100 mm on the west coast, because moist air comes mainly from the Indian Ocean in the east, is lifted by the escarpment and loses moisture moving west, while the west lies beside a cold current under high pressure. The national average is about 450 to 500 mm, making South Africa water-scarce.
